questions.question_text: Which unit is most appropriate for the volume of a single grain of sand?

options.why: Chose the unit that suits a sugar cube, which is far larger than a grain of sand.
Chose a fridge-sized unit, which would make a grain of sand a decimal with many leading zeros.

questions.solution_text:
A grain of sand is well under a millimetre across in every direction.
The cubic millimetre is the smallest cubic unit and is the one that matches it.
$\text{mm}^3$

questions.question_text: Which unit is most appropriate for the water held behind a large country dam?

options.why: Chose the unit that suits a backyard pool, so a dam would run to tens of thousands of units.
Chose the everyday unit for a milk bottle, giving a dam a count with ten or more digits.
Chose the unit for a teaspoon, the smallest on the ladder, giving a dam an unreadable count.

questions.solution_text:
A dam holds the water supply of a whole town.
The megalitre is the largest unit on the capacity ladder and is the one water authorities use.
ML

questions.question_text: Which of these is most likely to have a capacity of about $1$ kL?

options.why: Treated a kilolitre as a hand-held amount rather than a thousand litres.
Treated a kilolitre as dam-sized, when a farm dam holds megalitres.
Treated a kilolitre as a household basin, which holds only a few litres.

questions.solution_text:
One kilolitre is a thousand litres, about the amount in five full bathtubs.
A drink bottle and a sink hold far less, and a farm dam holds far more.
A small backyard rainwater tank.

questions.question_text: Which of these objects has a capacity as well as a volume?

options.why: Treated any object that takes up space as also able to hold liquid inside it.
Confused the space a solid takes up with the amount a container can hold.
Chose a solid object, which has a volume but nothing can be poured into it.

questions.solution_text:
Every one of these objects takes up space, so every one has a volume.
Only a hollow container can be filled, and the watering can is the only hollow one.
A watering can.

questions.question_text: Which list gives the units of capacity in order from largest to smallest?

options.why: Listed the units from smallest to largest instead of largest to smallest.
Placed the litre above the kilolitre, treating 'kilo' as smaller than the base unit.
Assumed a kilolitre is larger than a megalitre.

questions.solution_text:
Each step up the ladder is $1000$ times the one below it.
The megalitre is the largest and the millilitre is the smallest.
ML, kL, L, mL

questions.question_text: How many litres are equal to $1$ kL?

options.why: Used a step of $100$, the factor between centimetres and metres, rather than between litres and kilolitres.
Used the step of $10$ that separates units of length, not the $1000$ between capacity units.
Used the step from litres to megalitres instead of the step from litres to kilolitres.

questions.solution_text:
Each step up the capacity ladder is a thousand times larger.
A kilolitre is one step above a litre.
$1000$

questions.question_text: A swimming pool's capacity is recorded as $45\,000\,000$ mL. Which unit would present this capacity best?

options.why: Kept the recorded unit even though an eight-digit count cannot be pictured.
Jumped to the dam-sized unit, giving a single pool a decimal well below $1$.
Chose the everyday unit, giving a five-digit count for one backyard pool.

questions.solution_text:
An eight-digit count of millilitres is accurate but impossible to picture.
Kilolitres are the unit used for pools and turn the same capacity into the short whole number $45$.
kL

questions.question_text: A box has a volume of $1000\text{ cm}^3$. What is its capacity, in litres?

options.why: Treated each cubic centimetre as holding a litre rather than a millilitre.
Divided by $1000$ a second time after the count of litres had already been found.
Used a factor of $100$ between cubic centimetres and litres instead of $1000$.

questions.solution_text:
Each cubic centimetre of space holds one millilitre.
A thousand millilitres is one litre.
$1$ L

questions.question_text: A technical report records four measurements: a bead of solder, a bottle of soft drink, the air inside a shipping container, and the water in a suburb's supply. Which set of units is most appropriate, in that order?

options.why: Chose cubic centimetres for a bead of solder, which is only a few millimetres across, so its volume is a fraction of one cubic centimetre.
Chose kilolitres for a suburb's water supply, giving a count in the tens of thousands when megalitres is the reporting unit.
Makes both slips at once: steps up one size for the solder bead and down one size for the suburb's supply, so both ends of the report are off by a step.

questions.solution_text:
A bead of solder is a solid a few millimetres across: $\text{mm}^3$.
A soft-drink bottle holds a litre or two of liquid: L.
A shipping container encloses a space metres across: $\text{m}^3$.
A suburb's water supply is far more than a thousand kilolitres: ML.
Solids take cubic units and held liquids take litre units, and within each family the size closest to the object is chosen.
